glossary.convention: $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$ is represented either directly on the quotient or by fields on $\mathbb R^3$ invariant under all integer translations. Integrals and essential suprema use the closed unit-volume cube $[-1/2,1/2]^3$; its boundary has zero volume. Removing the torus origin means removing every point of $\mathbb Z^3$ from the covering space. Periodicity by itself imposes no regularity, parity, incompressibility or mean-zero condition.

On the unit torus, a frequency radius $\Lambda$ means vanishing Fourier coefficients at integer vectors $k$ with $|k|>\Lambda$. It counts the integer modes in $e^{2\pi i k\cdot x}$, rather than the vectors $2\pi k$. The zero mode of the inverse Laplacian is assigned zero. The Leray projection consequently preserves constant velocity modes.

A solution is jointly smooth on $[0,T_*)\times\mathbb R^3$, periodic in space, and satisfies Euler pointwise, with $0<T_*<\infty$. Maximality excludes a smooth solution on any larger such time interval agreeing in velocity on $[0,T_*)$. The value at time zero is included; the singular time is excluded. Values outside this interval are not part of the solution assertion.

A derivative within a time set uses only approaching times in that set. On a nondegenerate closed interval it is the ordinary interior derivative and the one-sided derivative at each endpoint. The Euler lifespan is $[0,T_*)$; the mean problem uses $[0,T]$, $0<T\le1$; active weighted estimates use $[t_0,T]$. Wave equations can be required on a compact set $I$ containing the physical interval. On arbitrary $I$, a supplied relative derivative need not be an unrestricted derivative; assertions using a uniquely determined derivative require the appropriate domain hypothesis.

Underlying fields have values at all real times, but regularity and equations are asserted only on their stated time sets. Some profile spaces use zero values outside the time slab. Such a convention does not imply smoothness through the endpoints after zero extension. Uniqueness of a solution on its interval does not determine arbitrary values outside it.

The unrestricted derivative expression is zero at a point where the function is not differentiable. A derivative within a set also has a specified zero value when the hypotheses needed to select a unique derivative fail. An equation containing these expressions alone does not establish differentiability. Under the actual smoothness, differentiability and domain hypotheses, they have their ordinary mathematical meanings.

Vectors in $\mathbb R^3$ have the Euclidean norm. The matrices $B,E_c$ in $\delta$ use its induced operator norm. Ordinary real pairs carry $\|(u,v)\|_\infty=\max(|u|,|v|)$, and coefficient errors use the induced pair operator norm. The reference propagator estimate with explicit square roots uses the Euclidean pair norm. Bounds on sums of absolute coordinates are stated as such. These conventions must not be silently interchanged when a numerical constant is quoted.

Real division assigns $x/0=0$. Thus $v/|v|=0$ at $v=0$, and a normalized vector has unit length only under $v\ne0$. The projection $P_\kappa=(\kappa\otimes\kappa)/|\kappa|^2$ is zero at $\kappa=0$, while $I-P_\kappa$ is the identity there. Equal-point Hölder quotients also contribute zero. These definitions do not justify cancellation of a denominator. Nonzero wave data, positive scales and positive active weights are supplied where their geometric interpretation is used.

Derivative orders, depths, radius exponents and frequency-separation exponents are nonnegative integers. Subtraction of such indices stops at zero. A range such as $n\ge1$ makes $5n-4$ equal to its ordinary integer value. The profile exponent $1-j$ and cutoff exponent $2-P$ are signed integers and can be negative. The hierarchy powers $-5/4-2(p-1)/3$, $-5/2-2(p-2)/3$ and $-9/4-2(p-1)/3$ use real subtraction. Fractional width and frequency powers have positive bases in the analytic applications.

A constant chosen before specified data is independent of those data. In the amplification bounds, a real factor $C$ and nonnegative integer exponent $p$ are chosen before the universal integer threshold for $C_0$ and before the wave data. The smallness condition uses the integer power $T^{C_0}$. The model limit instead fixes $\varepsilon,T$ and a tolerance before choosing its shear threshold. In the hierarchy, order-dependent constants may depend on their indicated orders and prescribed derivative bounds, while the parent exponent and radius threshold precede the later parent and frequency data. No analytic or Gevrey growth of an order-dependent sequence follows from these assertions.

At activation $t_0$, freeze $\sigma=|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|$, $
u>0$ and $\eta>0$, and put $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$, $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}>0$ and $S=\sigma/r$. The normalized time is $	au=r(t-t_0)$, with inverse $t=t_0+	au/r$. The interval $[0,T]$ in normalized time corresponds to $[t_0,t_0+T/r]$. The compact physical set $I$ can be larger; the wave equations are required throughout $I$ and the physical error is measured there.

The first two frame vectors are $E_1=k/|k|$ and $E_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, and the third is $E_3=E_1\times E_2$. For nonzero perpendicular data this fixes a positively oriented orthonormal frame. Its first, second and third formal positions correspond to paper indices $1,2,3$. The scalar $E_i\cdot BE_j$ uses the same row and column order as the paper. Reversing the cross product would reverse the third axis and the corresponding coupling sign.

In the preceding wave’s frame, $k=\lambda(\zeta_1E_1+\zeta_2E_2/S+\zeta_3E_3)$ and $\mathbf a=\alpha_1E_1/S+\alpha_2E_2+\alpha_3E_3/S$. Several intermediate equations act on $(U,V)=(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$. Returning to the paper’s coordinates conjugates the matrix by $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)$. The weighted quantity $m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2$ is $|k|^2/\lambda^2$, not the Euclidean squared norm of $\zeta$.

glossary.term: Reference angle and actual wave direction
glossary.convention: The reference angle is $\varphi(\tau)=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. It belongs to the limiting reference equation. The angle of the actual perturbed wave is a separate quantity; the estimates compare the wave with the reference and do not identify the angles exactly. The zero of the reference slope locates the reference maximum, not necessarily the maximum of the actual amplitude.

The reference turning time $\tau_m$ is the unique nonnegative zero of the Riccati slope and maximizes $a_{\rm ref}$. The crossing proposition separately asserts an attained maximum $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$ of the physical amplitude. It does not place that maximum at $\tau_m$ or assert a unique crossing. The numbered proposition characterizes $\tau_m$ using every reference solution; the older crossing theorem receives one reference solution as input and produces its turning time.

glossary.term: Reference amplitude and the interval integral
glossary.convention: The reference amplitude is $a_{\rm ref}(t)=\exp\int_0^tY$. The standard imported real interval integral reverses sign when its endpoints are reversed and is assigned zero when the integrand is not integrable; the latter assignment gives $a_{\rm ref}=1$. A differential equation or integrability assertion does not follow from that definition. Reference solutions are continuous on the half-line, so their integrals have the ordinary meaning.

The standard imported real square root is zero at nonpositive inputs, and its reciprocal is then zero. Thus $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ in the early-amplitude comparison means $1/\sqrt\varepsilon$ with that assigned value if $\varepsilon\le0$. That isolated comparison assumes only $2\varepsilon\le1$; the physical amplification application has $\varepsilon>0$.

glossary.term: Observation set for the physical error
glossary.convention: Each term in the physical error $\delta$ is a supremum over the entire compact set $I$. This is the paper's interval supremum when $I=[t_0,t_0+T/r]$. A larger $I$ can enlarge $\delta$, and the smallness conditions must then be checked on that larger set. Nonemptiness, compactness and continuity give the ordinary finite suprema used in the amplification estimates.

The unrestricted real supremum is assigned zero for an empty set or a set not bounded above. The finite derivative expressions use sets containing zero; their numerical value alone therefore does not establish boundedness. Analytic estimates require or prove bounded derivative sets. In the weighted expressions, the reciprocal contributes $|\gamma^{-1}|$; it is zero at $\gamma=0$. Positive scales and a positive weight are required for the ordinary weighted-norm interpretation.

glossary.term: Force, velocity and displacement in particle labels
glossary.convention: For a flow $X$, put $F=D_aX$ and $M=DU\circ X$. A physical force $f(t,x)$ becomes $f(t,X(t,a))$ in labels. A supplied function $f_{\rm lab}(t,a)$ is already a label force and is identified with $f\circ X$ only when that relation is given. If $v=z_t$, then $B=Fv$ is the correction in labels, $b=B\circ X^{-1}$ its Eulerian form, and $\xi=Fz$ the particle displacement. Arbitrary matrix data $F,M$ need not come from a specified flow.

A profile $f(t,a,s)$ has an independent label $a$ and phase $s$. Phase period one and $f(t,a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=f(t,a,s)$ give the required combined periodicity. Its physical value is $f^\natural(t,x)=f(t,X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(x),k_*\cdot X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(x))$. The carrier $k_*$ can be any real vector compatible with the stated hypotheses. Periodicity of the resulting physical field is supplied by the profile continuation, not by assuming $k_*\in\mathbb Z^3$.

A path $z\in H^1_0(0,T;\mathbb R^3)$ is represented as $z(t)=\int_0^tv(s)\,ds$ with $v\in L^2(0,T)$ and $\int_0^Tv=0$. This includes every Sobolev path with zero traces at both endpoints. Zero displacement does not mean zero initial velocity.

glossary.term: Upper bound for a quadratic form
glossary.convention: $H\le cI$ means $\langle Hw,w\rangle\le c|w|^2$ for every vector $w$. It is neither an absolute operator norm bound nor a symmetry assertion. The endpoint quantity is $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$. For a smooth approximate parent with its flow, $H^\#=(D_x^2p_U-D_xR_U)\circ X$. For an exact Euler parent, the residual term vanishes. Large negative eigenvalues are permitted by an upper bound.

The endpoint spatial $C^{0,1/2}$ norm is $\max(\|f\|_\infty,[f]_{1/2})$, followed by a supremum over the closed time interval. This is the norm on bounded half-Hölder fields in the authors' formalization. A solution estimate is $\|v\|\le A\|L\|$ for a specified source $L$; the inverse operator has norm at most $A$. The coefficient quantities in the quantitative estimate bound values and first spatial derivatives, rather than full $C^{1,1/2}$ norms.

The spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm sums, for derivative orders zero through $m$, the supremum norm and the one-half Hölder seminorm of the corresponding full multilinear spatial derivative, using its operator norm. A time-uniform bound takes the supremum in time of that spatial norm. It is not a space-time Hölder norm. Uniform derivative bounds through $m+1$ give the displayed regularity and the explicit factor $3(m+1)$ in the physical-evaluation estimate.

For positive $\ell_*,h$, the finite profile norm is $\|f\|_{[n]}=\sum_{|\alpha|+j\le n}\ell_*^{|\alpha|}h^j\sup_{[0,T],a,s}|\partial_a^\alpha\partial_s^jf|$. The weighted version uses $[t_0,T]$ and divides by the positive $\gamma(t)$ after label and phase differentiation. Each multiindex is counted once. No time derivatives occur. For a phase-independent field the phase derivatives of positive order vanish.

The physical derivative sum in Lemma 5.7 ranges over all coordinate sequences of length $m$. Equal mixed derivatives can occur more than once. It dominates the paper's multi-index sum, and the multiplicity depends only on $m$. This convention does not apply to the finite profile norm, which counts each multi-index once.

The Euler and truncated Poisson pressures are normalized by zero spatial mean. Transverse pressures instead have zero phase mean. The continuous-source endpoint equation determines a periodic pressure gradient; its scalar potential admits a time-dependent additive constant and is not thereby time differentiable. A chosen zero-mean potential fixes that freedom. The smooth-force theorem reconstructs a smooth, zero-mean label pressure; it does not identify it with the negative time derivative of an arbitrary earlier potential. The periodic inverse Laplacian removes the constant Fourier mode.

The paper selects the spatial mean-zero Poisson pressure. The formal parent hypotheses in Section 5 allow any smooth periodic pressure whose residual satisfies the required oddness, Fourier, size and quadratic-form conditions; they do not separately impose a Poisson equation or divergence freedom of the residual. The new pressure after Fourier truncation is explicitly the normalized Poisson pressure.

With $\gamma(t)=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|$, stability quantifies over every transverse homogeneous solution $b$ and every $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$: $|b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|b(t')|/\gamma(t')$. The selected seed alone does not express this control. The formal normalization is $0<\gamma\le1$; the paper additionally fixes the attained maximum to be one. The normalized coupling inequality is a separate hypothesis.

For continuous $f$, put $Jf(s)=\int_0^sf(r)\,dr$ and $\partial_s^{-1}f=Jf-\int_0^1Jf$. This primitive has zero phase mean. It is one-periodic when $f$ is one-periodic with zero phase mean, and need not vanish at phase zero. The formula also accepts other inputs, for which periodicity or an ordinary derivative need not follow.

The formal construction selects a particular smooth cutoff $g(a)=\chi(|a|/\ell_*)$. For $\ell_*>0$, it is one on $|a|\le\ell_*$ and zero on $|a|\ge2\ell_*$. It does not quantify over every admissible cutoff. At $\ell_*=0$, division by zero gives $g\equiv1$, so positivity is essential for localization.

The cutoff is smooth on $[0,T]$, takes values in $[0,1]$, and vanishes for $t<t_0$ within that interval. It need not eventually equal one. The first wave takes $t_0=0$ and the constant cutoff one. No smoothness or vanishing outside the slab is asserted merely by the cutoff definition.

The correction stored with $V_p$ is the paper's $C_{p+1}$. The paper index is recovered by natural-number predecessor, so the bare definition gives $C_0=C_1$. The finite expansion separately requires $C_1=0$ and retains $C_{P+1}$ while imposing $V_{P+1}=B_{P+1}=0$.

The real logarithm is assigned zero at zero and extended to negative arguments using absolute value. The parameter hypotheses force the relevant frequencies and thresholds to be positive, so their logarithms have the ordinary meaning. The formula $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$ alone does not establish that positivity.

The gradient and vorticity $L^\infty$ quantities in the singularity statement are essential suprema on the unit cell, with values in $[0,\infty]$. Their nonnegative time integrals can equal infinity. These are distinct from the real supremum expressions used in some finite-norm definitions, whose exceptional default is zero. Smooth periodic fields have finite spatial suprema at each fixed time before the singular endpoint; the time integrals can nevertheless diverge.

glossary.term: The unit torus and periodic lifts
glossary.convention: The spatial domain is $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$, with measure of total mass one and Fourier modes $e^{2\pi i k\cdot x}$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^3$. A periodic lift is unchanged by integer translations. Every lattice point represents the single torus origin, so the punctured torus is represented by $\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Z^3$. A lifted observation set must avoid that whole lattice. A support condition within distance $r$ of the lattice represents a ball about the torus origin. A lifted flow satisfies $X(t,a+n)=X(t,a)+n$: its displacement, rather than its position, is periodic.

glossary.term: Distances on the torus and the lift
glossary.convention: The lift $\mathbb R^3$ carries Euclidean distance. The direct torus used in the endpoint spaces carries the product metric $d_\infty$, the maximum of the three circle distances. If $d_2$ is the Euclidean quotient metric, then $d_\infty\le d_2\le\sqrt3\,d_\infty$. Consequently $[f]_{1/2,d_2}\le[f]_{1/2,d_\infty}\le3^{1/4}[f]_{1/2,d_2}$. The Euclidean seminorm of a periodic lift agrees with the $d_2$ seminorm after minimizing over lattice translates, but not in general with the $d_\infty$ seminorm. The quotient map from the Euclidean lift to the product-metric torus is nonexpanding.

On a nondegenerate interval $[a,b]$, time derivatives use times in that interval: right derivatives at $a$, left derivatives at $b$ and ordinary derivatives inside. For a physical velocity the spatial point is fixed during this differentiation. On $[0,T)$ there is no derivative condition at the excluded endpoint $T$. A condition on a general compact time set uses derivatives relative to that set, which need not be an interval. Fields and derivative expressions are defined at other times as well; their notation alone imposes neither an equation nor differentiability there. In the cutoff commutation assertion, the symbol and frequency scale are fixed in time.

Orders, depths and the schedule exponent $K(s)=320b(s+1)$ are nonnegative integers. The recurrence is $\lambda_0=N$, $q_1=1$ and $\lambda_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{K(q_j)}$ for $j\ge1$, with ordinary integer powers and $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$. Subtraction within the nonnegative integers stops at zero. Thus $q-1$ in the mean-source estimate means $\max(q-1,0)$, and the otherwise unused $\tau_0$ formula uses $\lambda_0$ in place of $\lambda_{-1}$. Under $j\ge1$, $j-1$ is the ordinary difference. Internal step $i$ constructs paper wave $j=i+1$, so depth $6K(q_{i+2})$ is $6K_{j+1}$. The tail exponent $s-M$ is instead formed as a signed integer difference and may be negative.

Negative and fractional analytic exponents, such as $\lambda^{-3/4}$ and $\lambda^{-1/8}$, are real exponents. For $\lambda>0$ they have their usual meaning. In the numerical remainder identity the allowed case $\lambda=0$ follows $0^0=1$ and $0^r=0$ for nonzero real $r$; it has no zero-frequency-wave interpretation. The expression $2-P$ in the Fourier-tail exponent is subtraction in the real numbers and may be negative.

Vectors in $\mathbb R^3$ carry the Euclidean norm. A matrix acting on vectors carries the induced operator norm. With $(\nabla U)_{ij}=\partial_jU_i$, its action is $D_xU\,v$, and $(a\otimes k)v=(k\cdot v)a$. Thus $\|a\otimes k\|=|a||k|$. For the rank-one stationary shear matrix this operator norm equals its Frobenius norm. Full higher spatial derivatives carry the corresponding multilinear operator norm.

When $T=0$, the interval $[0,T]$ is the singleton $\{0\}$. Any proposed derivative satisfies the derivative condition relative to that singleton; it imposes no time evolution. The first-wave initial values, nonvanishing and attained maximum at zero still constrain the data. The numbered Lemma 6.1 assumes $T>0$, whereas its more general existence statements allow $T=0$.

For nonzero perpendicular covector $\kappa$ and amplitude $\mathbf a$, set $E_1=\kappa/|\kappa|$, $E_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$ and $E_3=E_1\times E_2$. This is an orthonormal frame. The entries of $B$ are $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$, with $\nu=B_{12}$ and $\eta=B_{32}$. Source coordinates numbered zero, one and two correspond to the paper's one, two and three.

glossary.term: Positive denominators and division by zero
glossary.convention: Division is defined even at a zero denominator, with $a/0=0$. Consequently a normalized-vector formula alone does not imply unit length. In the central-wave results, nonzero covectors and amplitudes and positive frozen couplings make the divisions by $|\kappa|$, $|\mathbf a|$, $\nu$ and $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$ ordinary divisions by positive numbers. Those hypotheses must accompany any use of the normalized frame or weighted amplitude ratio.

glossary.term: Normalized time and frozen growth scale
glossary.convention:
At activation, freeze positive strength $\sigma$ and coupling $
u$, and set $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $S=\sigma/r$. Normalized time is $	au=r(t-t_0)$, with inverse $t=t_0+	au/r$. Hence $[0,\Theta]$ corresponds to $[t_0,t_0+\Theta/r]$ and one normalized time unit lasts $1/r$. The exact frozen growth rate, when $\sigma>
u$, is $r\sqrt{1-
u/\sigma}$.

Saying that the peak is $U_*$ means both $|\mathbf a(t)|\le U_*$ at every time of the specified closed interval and equality at some time there. It is not merely an upper bound. The first wave uses $U_*=\lambda^{-3/4}$; the general growing-wave data permit an independent prescribed peak, specialized to that value in the induction.

The recurrence chooses the greatest integer $s$ satisfying $1\le s\le q_j+1$ and $\mathcal B(s)\le\lambda_{j-1}$, not just an admissible integer. The greatest element belongs to that set and dominates every other member. The values $q_0$ and $\mathcal B(0)$ have no role in this recurrence. Arithmetic growth results can omit monotonicity and analytic-cost domination of $\mathcal B$ even though the paper imposes both on its chosen schedule.

The numbered common-sequence assertion fixes a Fourier symbol, then allows any integer floor $a_0$ and chooses $b\ge1$, an exponent $a\ge a_0$ and a majorant of fixed-order constants. The threshold function $\mathcal B$ is quantified afterward, and the lower bound for the initial frequency may depend on it. Thus the exponent can be chosen arbitrarily large; the conclusion does not say that every sufficiently large exponent works. The shorter existence theorem chooses just one threshold function.

glossary.term: Pointwise time bounds and time continuity
glossary.convention: An estimate imposed for every $t\in[0,S]$ gives a uniform numerical bound in time. By itself it does not assert continuity of the map from time into the spatial normed space. In particular the clause bounding the spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ size of each correction is distinct from the paper's explicit $C([0,S];C^{m,1/2})$ assertion. The spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm is $\sum_{i\le m}(\sup|D^if|+[D^if]_{1/2})$, where $D^if$ is the full $i$th derivative tensor in operator norm.

The inequality $D^2\pi_j\le A I$ means $v\cdot D^2\pi_j(t,x)v\le A|v|^2$ for every vector $v$. It is an upper bound as a quadratic form, not a bound for the norm or the absolute values of all Hessian entries. The sum $\sum_{i<j}\lambda_i^{-1}$ is the paper's $\sum_{i=1}^{j}\lambda_{i-1}^{-1}$; at $j=0$ it is empty and equals zero.

The selected crossing is least among the times in the closed bracket $[\tau_m,2(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}]$ at which the successor coupling ratio equals $\varepsilon_+$. Here $\tau_m$ is the reference turning time and $\tau$ is normalized time. The assertion does not exclude crossings before that bracket. Physical times are obtained by $t=t_0+\tau/r$.

glossary.term: Closed stage intervals and the lifespan
glossary.convention: An approximate stage is studied on $[0,S_j]$ and includes both endpoints. The Euler solution satisfies the equations on $[0,T_*)$ with $0<T_*<\infty$. Its functions are defined at other times, but that imposes no equation or smoothness there. An assertion about a continuous terminal velocity specifies its value at $T_*$ separately.

For a profile $f(t,a,s)$, time differentiation fixes the label $a$ and independent phase $s$. After substituting $a=X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(x)$ and $s=k_*\cdot a$, it becomes the material derivative $\partial_t+U\cdot\nabla_x$. It is distinct from differentiation at fixed physical position; conversion to that derivative introduces parent-velocity and spatial derivative factors.

The $L^\infty$ measurement is the essential supremum over $[-1/2,1/2]^3$ and can take the value $+\infty$. A spatial derivative is measured in the Euclidean operator norm, and higher full derivatives in the corresponding multilinear operator norm. For a smooth periodic field the essential supremum equals the ordinary supremum. Sums of coordinate partial-derivative norms can change fixed order-dependent constants.

The spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ measurement is a sum, through order $m$, of the supremum and half-Hölder seminorm of each full spatial derivative. This sum is visible in the supplied proofs, and derivatives use multilinear operator norms. A separate condition supplies finiteness. The defining file for the underlying Hölder quotient is absent, so its exact domain and zero-increment convention remain unverified here. This spatial norm must not be identified with the maximum norm used in the endpoint space.

The gradient and vorticity integrals are nonnegative Lebesgue integrals over $[0,T_*)$, with values in $[0,+\infty]$. Equality to $+\infty$ is integral divergence; the integral is not assigned a finite fallback value when the integrand is nonintegrable. A full limit of central vorticity to infinity alone does not imply divergence of this time integral.

For $T>0$ and a spatial seminorm $N$, $\mathcal J_q(f)=\sum_{i=0}^q T^iN(\partial_t^if)/i!$. Time differentiation fixes label and independent phase. In an amplitude-weighted measurement, division by the positive central amplitude occurs after differentiating the profile; the amplitude is not differentiated. Extracting order $i\le q$ costs $i!T^{-i}$.

For every fixed pair of derivative orders $(m,q)$ there may be a different starting stage. The assertion does not supply one starting stage for all orders at once. Likewise, constants and parent exponents in an eventual absorption estimate are fixed before the stage index tends to infinity; their permissible dependence follows their position in the quantifiers.

The maximal-solution comparison quantifies over a real $T>0$, hence a finite lifespan. Maximality means that no smooth periodic Euler solution on any longer interval agrees in velocity throughout $[0,T)$. An infinite lifespan is not a possible value of this parameter. This convention limits the literal comparison assertion even when a separate argument excludes a global continuation of the constructed example.

The assertion $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$ as $t\uparrow T_*$ means that every fixed lower threshold is exceeded at every sufficiently late time in $[0,T_*)$. It is stronger than unboundedness along a sequence. The formal Proposition 8.2 additionally retains a uniform lower bound throughout each sufficiently late activation interval.

glossary.term: Spatial limits and smooth time extension
glossary.convention: Local spatial limits for $u$ and $\partial_tu$ require convergence of their spatial derivatives on every compact set away from the origin. A jointly smooth velocity extension through the terminal time requires all mixed derivatives and is a separate assertion. The extension agrees before the terminal time and is periodic; neither a pressure extension nor the Euler equations after that time are required.

The matrix $\mathbf a\otimes\kappa$ acts on $v$ by $(\kappa\cdot v)\mathbf a$. Its vorticity contribution is $\kappa\times\mathbf a$ with the usual orientation. Its projection along $\kappa$ is zero. The ordering of the tensor factors fixes the sign of this identity.

For a half-Hölder field $f$ on the unit torus, the endpoint norm is $\max\{\sup_a\|f(a)\|,\sup_{a\ne b}\|f(a)-f(b)\|/d(a,b)^{1/2}\}$. Here $d$ is the product metric on the direct torus. The value and increment bounds use the same constant. This is the norm on the projected endpoint spaces; higher derivative norms in the sequence estimates are separate quantities.

The formal time measure is Lebesgue measure restricted to $(0,T]$. For $T>0$, identifying functions equal almost everywhere gives the ordinary $L^2(0,T)$ space; inclusion of endpoints does not change that space. A path with zero time integral has a primitive in $H^1_0(0,T)$. If $T\le0$, this restricted measure is zero.

Write $Jv(t)=\int_0^tv(s)\,ds$ for the oriented vector-valued integral. On a positive finite interval, continuous curves in the complete function spaces used by the endpoint argument have the usual primitive. The expression has value zero for nonintegrable inputs; in a noncomplete target the integral is also assigned zero. Default values do not assert a fundamental theorem of calculus.

The time norm is the real supremum of $\{\|f(t)\|:0\le t\le T\}$. Empty or unbounded sets have assigned supremum zero in this real-valued expression. For a continuous curve on $[0,T]$ with $T\ge0$, compactness makes it the ordinary finite supremum. It must not be used as an extended infinite norm.

The four nonnegative numbers $K_0,K_1,\Omega_0,\Omega_1$ are supplied uniform bounds on coefficients and their first spatial derivatives. They are not defined to be their least bounds. The formal parameter $2+\kappa^{-1}+\mu^{-1}+K_0+K_1+\Omega_0+\Omega_1$ can be bounded by the paper's full Hölder parameter with suitable choices of these numbers; no converse bound on first-derivative Hölder seminorms follows.

For a projection $\mathcal R$, the inverse acts on $\{v:\mathcal Rv=v\}$. In Appendix A the spatial choice is Leray projection onto weakly divergence-free fields. The time-path choice also subtracts the time average. A coefficient inverse on this space is not an inverse on every half-Hölder field. Some auxiliary statements use fixed vectors of a bounded map without assuming that map is a projection.

The spatial Leray symbol is $I-\widehat\xi\otimes\widehat\xi$ for $\xi\ne0$. The normalized zero vector is assigned zero, so the zero-frequency symbol is the identity and preserves spatial constants. In the time-path setting the zero-frequency action still includes subtraction of the time average.

For positive $r$, use $\chi(a)=\max\{0,\min\{1,2-d(a,a_0)/r\}\}$. It equals one on the closed $r$-ball, vanishes at distances at least $2r$, and has Lipschitz constant $r^{-1}$. It need not have a classical derivative at the transition radii. At $r=0$ the division convention makes it identically one, so localization requires $r>0$.

Bounds for Fourier operators built from the frozen symbols are distinct from identifying those operators with $A_0(D)^{-1}$ and $A_0(D)^{-1}\mathcal R$. The separate Fourier identity assumes the projection symbol is homogeneous of degree zero away from zero. The spatial Leray symbol and its time-path version have this property in the paper.

The cutoff is the finite sum over $|\xi|\le2\Lambda$ with coefficients $\psi(\xi/\Lambda)\widehat f(\xi)$. For $\Lambda>0$ and a symbol supported in the radius-two ball this is the usual multiplier. For other symbols the explicit band restriction still applies. At zero scale division is assigned zero; that value is outside the paper's positive-scale assumptions. Radiality implies evenness, whereas evenness alone allows nonradial symbols.

glossary.term: Real part of the spectral kernel
glossary.convention: For a real target, the separate general cutoff integrates the real part of $\sum_{|k|\le2\Lambda}\psi(k/\Lambda)e^{2\pi i k\cdot(x-z)}$ against the input. An even real symbol gives the intended multiplier; a non-even symbol is replaced by its even part in this real action. This construction does not require choosing a complexification of an arbitrary real target.

The Banach-valued $L^\infty$ hypothesis includes almost-everywhere strong measurability and an essentially bounded norm. Here the measurability requirement is approximation almost everywhere by measurable simple functions. Ordinary vector-valued integration is interpreted in a complete normed target. Some helper estimates omit completeness; their formal integration convention assigns zero in an incomplete target. A numerical inequality for that assigned value is not an ordinary integral theorem in every incomplete space.

glossary.term: Integral values outside the integrable case
glossary.convention: The real and vector integral expressions are defined even when an integrand is not integrable, using zero in that case. An integral identity without an integrability hypothesis therefore does not establish integrability. For the cutoff kernel and its moments, the Schwartz property supplies actual integrability; for the phase operators the paper uses smooth finite-dimensional profiles.

glossary.term: Integer difference in the tail exponent
glossary.convention: In $\Lambda^{s-M}$, the orders $s,M$ are nonnegative integers but their difference is formed as an integer. Thus for $s<M$ and $\Lambda>0$, the factor is $\Lambda^{-(M-s)}$. It is not the truncated natural-number difference, which would incorrectly give exponent zero.

The coefficient estimates use a nonnegative integer $q$ in $\mathsf D^{q(m+1)}$. For $\mathsf D\ge1$, a real exponent may be enlarged to an integer for a closure estimate. In the fixed-radius assertion of Lemma D.2(c), however, changing $C$ to $q=\lceil C\rceil$ changes both $\ell_*\le\mathsf D^{-C}$ and the powers in the conclusion. Products use $2\max(q,r)$ and inverses $3\max(q,e)$.

For positive scales, $\|f\|_{[n]}=\sum_{|\beta|+j\le n}\ell_*^{|\beta|}h^j\sup_{t,a,s}|\partial_a^\beta\partial_s^jf|$. Each mixed multi-index occurs once. The time set is an explicit parameter, commonly $[t_0,T]$ or a closed subinterval; time is not differentiated. For a phase-independent field only $j=0$ contributes. The expressions use real-valued suprema and require bounded derivative families for their ordinary norm interpretation.

The weighted norm is the finite derivative norm of $f(t,a,s)/\gamma(t)$. For the paper, $\gamma>0$ on $[t_0,T]$; the estimates require bounded derivatives of this quotient. Positivity on an arbitrary time set does not itself give a positive lower bound for $\gamma$. The unrestricted formula assigns zero to the normalized field at any time with $\gamma=0$.

For the finite norms of Appendix D, each derivative contributes the supremum over time of $\max\{\|g(t)\|_\infty,[g(t)]_{1/2}\}$, with $[g]_{1/2}=\sup_{a\ne b}|g(a)-g(b)|/|a-b|^{1/2}$. The coincident-point quotient is assigned zero. The sum convention lies between this maximum and twice it. The separate spatial Hölder norms described in Appendix B sum uniform and half-Hölder bounds of derivative tensors; the two conventions should not be silently identified.

A full spatial derivative tensor is measured in its multilinear operator norm. The quantities $|c|_m$ of Appendix D instead sum the suprema of coordinate derivatives with $|\beta|=m$, counting each multi-index once. The supplied equivalence changes constants depending on $m$ in spatial dimension three, while preserving the exponent of $\mathsf D$. It does not identify the numerical norms or give constants uniform across a family unless those quantifiers are stated.

For arbitrary direction fields or linear derivative maps, a nondecreasing sequence specifies one chosen order of composition. The maps need not commute, so this is not automatically an ordinary mixed partial derivative. Constant coordinate derivatives commute and then give one representative per multi-index. The low-level lifting estimate needs forcing derivatives to commute; the numbered statement additionally uses commuting coefficient derivatives to pass from an exact-order sum to each individual composition.

The phase has period one. Its mean is $\int_0^1f(s)\,ds$, and the normalized primitive is $\int_0^sf(r)\,dr-\int_0^1\int_0^qf(r)\,dr\,dq$. For continuous Banach-valued input it has derivative $f$ and zero mean; it is periodic when the input is periodic with zero mean. The normalization fixes the mean, not the value at phase zero. The primitive bound is two times the supremum bound on one period.

A bound with constants selected after a field and parent parameter are fixed does not by itself state uniformity over those choices. In the numbered coefficient lemma, the input constant sequences, value spaces and integer exponents are fixed first; output constants are then chosen before the time domain, parent parameter and fields. In the abstract lifting lemma the constant is selected before the derivative maps, although it may depend on the number of derivative directions.

The formal real logarithm is $\log|x|$ when $x\ne0$ and is zero at $x=0$. This convention makes the three-step logarithmic identity meaningful without a positivity hypothesis. In Appendix C the actual frequencies exceed one, so it is the ordinary real logarithm and the extension does not change the estimate.

showcase.why: Proves the three schedule properties of Lemma 1.3, including (1.15), assuming only $\mathcal B(s)>0$ and the lower bound (1.13).
showcase.text: Let $b\ge1$ be an integer and $K(s)=320b(s+1)$. Assume $\mathcal B(s)>0$ and $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$ for $s\ge1$, $q_1=1$, $\lambda_0\ge\mathcal B(1)$, $\lambda_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{K(q_j)}$, and $q_{j+1}=\max\{1\le s\le q_j+1:\mathcal B(s)\le\lambda_{j-1}\}$ for $j\ge1$. The formal statement proves $q_j\le q_{j+1}\le q_j+1$, $q_j\to\infty$, and $4\log\lambda_{j+2}\le(\log\lambda_{j-1})^2$ for every $j\ge1$. The last formula is exactly (1.15), since $L_i=4\log\lambda_{i+1}$. The maximum is the greatest admissible integer. In the paper, $\mathcal B$ is also nondecreasing and dominates the fixed-order analytic constants, and $b$ is fixed by the later construction. The formal statement does not assume these two conditions; it proves the same three assertions from $\mathcal B(s)>0$ and the lower bound (1.13) alone. Frequencies are real, while derivative orders and the exponents $K(s)$ are nonnegative integers; the hypotheses force the relevant frequencies to be positive.

showcase.why: Proves $2/\varepsilon\le\tan\varphi(\tau_m)\le9/(2\varepsilon)$ for every $\varepsilon>0$; the card derives $\cos\varphi(\tau_m)$ comparable to $\varepsilon$ when $\varepsilon\le1$.
showcase.text: For $\varepsilon>0$ and $\tau_m\in[2/\varepsilon,3/\varepsilon]$, put $\varphi(\tau)=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. The formal statement proves $2/\varepsilon\le\tan\varphi(\tau_m)\le9/(2\varepsilon)$. It assumes only the displayed time bracket; it does not assert that $\tau_m$ is a zero of a reference slope or a maximum of an amplitude. The resulting cosine bounds are $\varepsilon/\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+81/4}\le\cos\varphi(\tau_m)\le\varepsilon/\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+4}$. Concluding that this cosine is comparable to $\varepsilon$ requires an upper bound on $\varepsilon$, such as $\varepsilon\le1$, which the paper’s application supplies but this statement does not assume. No differential equation or amplitude estimate is used in this scalar calculation.

showcase.why: Lists the conditions defining a smooth mean solution for given matrix fields $F,M$, and when those fields come from an actual flow.
showcase.text: On $[0,T]$, let $F,M$ be smooth unit-periodic matrix fields, and let $G$ satisfy $GF=FG=I$. Assume $F_t=MF$, $\|G\|\le D$, $\|M\|\le L$, and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$. Put $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. For a supplied label force $f_{\rm lab}$, a smooth mean solution consists of smooth unit-periodic fields $v,z,B,\mathsf q$ satisfying $z_t=v$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, $\operatorname{div}_av=0$, $B=Fv$ and $B_t+MB+G^T\nabla_a\mathsf q=f_{\rm lab}$ on the closed interval. These are defining conditions, not an existence assertion. No spatial mean normalization of $\mathsf q$ is imposed. An actual flow is not part of these data. Only after separately identifying $F=D_aX$, $M=DU\circ X$ and $f_{\rm lab}=f\circ X$ may one interpret $Fz$ as particle displacement and $B\circ X^{-1}$ as the Eulerian correction.

showcase.why: States the forced Jacobi inverse with its hypotheses and solution spaces; the constant $A$ is polynomial in supremum bounds on $K,\Omega,D_aK,D_a\Omega$.
showcase.text: Let $0<T\le1$, $D\ge1$ and $L_0\ge0$. On $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, take smooth matrix fields $F,M$ satisfying $F_t=MF$, with $F^{-1}$ defined, $\|F^{-1}\|\le D$, $\|M\|\le L_0$ and $-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ as a quadratic form. Put $K=F^TF$ and $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. Suppose the nonnegative constants $K_0,K_1,\Omega_0,\Omega_1$ bound $\|K\|,\|D_aK\|,\|\Omega\|,\|D_a\Omega\|$ uniformly in the Euclidean operator norms. There is a universal $C\ge0$, chosen before all these data, with $A=C(D+L_0+K_0+K_1+\Omega_0+\Omega_1)^{1164}$. For every $L\in C([0,T];C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3))$, the formal statement supplies unique divergence-free $v\in C([0,T];C^{0,1/2})$ and $c\in C^{0,1/2}$ satisfying $Kv-\int_0^t\Omega v+L=c+\nabla_a\phi$, where $c$ is independent of time, $z(t)=\int_0^tv$, $z(0)=z(T)=0$, and $\phi$ has zero mean with $\nabla_a\phi\in C([0,T];C^{0,1/2})$. It gives $\|v\|_{C_tC^{0,1/2}}\le A\|L\|_{C_tC^{0,1/2}}$ and $\|(\mathbb P K(t))^{-1}\mathbb P\|\le A$, where $\mathbb P$ is the Leray projection and the inverse acts on divergence-free fields. The spatial Hölder norm is the maximum of supremum and seminorm. The polynomial uses supremum bounds for the coefficients and their first derivatives; the paper uses their larger $C^{1,1/2}$ norms. The abstract fields $F,M$ need not have been obtained from a specified flow.

showcase.why: Gives the graph bounds (5.44) and (5.45) for a profile already extended across cell faces, with any real normed target.
showcase.text:
Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$ and $\lambda\ge1$. The parent $U$ is a smooth odd divergence-free field on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, with Fourier support $|\xi|\le2\mathsf D$ and flow $X$. The bounds $\|\nabla U\|_\infty,\|D_aX\|_\infty,\|(D_aX)^{-1}\|_\infty\le\mathsf D$ hold. For a smooth periodic pressure $p_U$, set $R_U=U_t+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla p_U$; require $R_U$ odd, supported in $|\xi|\le4\mathsf D$, $\|R_U\|_\infty\le\lambda^{-5/2}$, and $D^2p_U-\nabla R_U\le I$ as quadratic forms. The formal statement imposes these conditions directly. The paper selects the zero-mean Poisson pressure; the formal statement permits any pressure meeting the displayed conditions, without separately requiring $\operatorname{div}R_U=0$.

Write $F=D_aX$, $M=(\nabla U)\circ X$ and $\kappa=F^{-T}k_*$, where $k_*\ne0$. Choose $0\le t_0<T$ with $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda$. At the origin take a nonzero transverse solution $\mathbf a$ of $\mathbf a_t=-M\mathbf a+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$. Put $\gamma(t)=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|$. For every transverse homogeneous solution $\mathbf b$ and $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$, assume $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$, and assume $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$ at the origin. The formal normalization is $0<\gamma\le1$; the paper additionally requires $\max\gamma=1$. Fix $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$ for a sufficiently large integer $a$, and $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$.

For a profile $f(t,a,s)$, the norm $\|f\|_{[n]}$ sums $\ell_*^{|\alpha|}h^j\sup|\partial_a^\alpha\partial_s^j f|$ over $|\alpha|+j\le n$ on $[0,T]$. The weighted norm $\|f\|_{[n],\gamma}$ uses $[t_0,T]$ and divides by $\gamma(t)$; it differentiates only labels and phase. Each multi-index is counted once. The profiles are smooth on the closed time slab, one-periodic in $s$, and satisfy $f(t,a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=f(t,a,s)$ for $n\in\mathbb Z^3$. Their stipulated zero values outside the time slab do not assert smoothness across its endpoints.

Let $g_0$ be such a profile with values in a real normed space, independent of phase outside the repeated support of the envelope. Here $g(a)=\chi(|a|/\ell_*)$ uses the fixed smooth radial cutoff, equal to one for $|a|\le\ell_*$ and zero for $|a|\ge2\ell_*$, with its support repeated over the label lattice. Define its physical field by $g_0^\natural(t,x)=g_0(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ with $a=X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(x)$. The transformation rule of the profile ensures periodicity in $x$ even when $k_*\notin\mathbb Z^3$. For $t\in[t_0,T]$, the formal statement bounds the sum of its order-$m$ spatial derivative suprema by $C_m(\mathsf D^C\lambda^{3/2})^m\gamma(t)\|g_0\|_{[m],\gamma}$ and gives $\|g_0^\natural(t)\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le C_m(\mathsf D^C\lambda^{3/2})^{m+1}\gamma(t)\|g_0\|_{[m+1],\gamma}$, including membership in $C^{m,1/2}$. This spatial norm sums the supremum and one-half Hölder seminorm of the full multilinear derivatives through order $m$, using their operator norms.

The same bounds hold on $[0,T]$ with the unweighted norm and $\gamma$ replaced by one. If $g_0$ is independent of phase everywhere, the factor $\lambda^{3/2}$ per derivative disappears. The formal spatial derivative sum in the conclusion ranges over all ordered coordinate sequences of length $m$; the paper's sum ranges over multi-indices. Their multiplicities are bounded in terms of $m$ and absorbed into $C_m$. This physical derivative sum is distinct from the finite profile norm on the right, which counts each multi-index once.

The numbered formal statement starts with a profile defined for all labels and phases, smooth on $[0,T]$, and satisfying the coupled translation law. The paper starts with cell data whose phase average extends smoothly and periodically across the faces. Thus the numbered formal statement does not itself construct a global profile from those cell data. A separate statement constructs smooth periodic physical evaluation at a fixed time under an explicit collar condition: the profile agrees there with a smooth periodic mean. The paper's compact support in the interior of the label cell furnishes this collar; it is not a new substantive restriction. That separate statement does not assert joint smoothness in time in this form. The estimates agree once the cell data have been extended. The formal statement also allows arbitrary real normed target spaces, asserts the Hölder regularity explicitly, and uses the broader parent and seed hypotheses above. The envelope exponent is fixed first, followed by $C$ and the sequence $C_m$, before the parent and target space. The integer $C$ is independent of derivative order and no expansion depth enters this estimate.

The verdict different records both directions of change. The arbitrary target space, ordered derivative sum, and larger parent and seed classes broaden the estimates. The numbered formal statement takes the resulting smooth continuation as input, while the paper also derives it from the support and phase-mean hypotheses. The powers of $\mathsf D$ and $\lambda$, the loss of one derivative for the Hölder estimate, and the distinction between the active weighted and full unweighted intervals agree.

showcase.text:
Let nonzero perpendicular $k_p,a_p$ solve $k_p'=-B^Tk_p$, $a_p'=-(I-2P_{k_p})Ba_p$ on a compact interval, where $P_{k_p}$ projects onto $\mathbb Rk_p$, $B$ is continuous and trace free, and $E$ is a continuous matrix error. Set $E_1=k_p/|k_p|$, $E_2=a_p/|a_p|$, $E_3=E_1	imes E_2$. At $t_0$ put $\sigma=|k_p||a_p|$, $
u=E_1\cdot BE_2>0$, $\eta=E_3\cdot BE_2>0$, $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $S=\sigma/r$, $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$. Assume $[t_0,t_0+H/r]$ lies in that interval, $H\ge2$, integer $C_0\ge240$, $C_0\varepsilon\le1$ and $C_0H^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$. The selected crossing wave starts at $\kappa(t_0)=\lambda E_3$, $\lambda
e0$, and solves $\kappa'=-(B+a_p\otimes k_p+E)^T\kappa$. Writing $\kappa/\lambda=\zeta_1E_1+(\zeta_2/S)E_2+\zeta_3E_3$, the formal statement gives $|\zeta_1|\le H^2$, $|\zeta_2|\le H$, $|\zeta_3-1|\le1/2$ on that physical window. These differ from the paper's time-dependent length bound. Here $\delta$ is the comparison error (2.6), with suprema over that compact interval.

showcase.why: Shows that inverses of operator-norm continuous invertible operators are continuous, then applies this to $S(t)v=\mathbb P(K(t)v)$ in Appendix A.2.
showcase.text: Let $X$ be a real Banach space and let $S(t):X\to X$ be bounded linear isomorphisms for every real $t$. If their forward operators vary continuously in operator norm on a prescribed set $I$, then their inverses vary continuously in operator norm on $I$. No common bound on the inverse norms is a hypothesis of this statement. In Appendix A.2, take $I=[0,1]$ and $S(t)v=\mathbb P(K(t)v)$ on divergence-free $C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3)$ fields. The fixed-time inverse must first be constructed, and continuity of the forward family must be established; the theorem then supplies continuity of the inverse family.

showcase.why: Gives the $L^\infty$ bound $\|\check\psi\|_{L^1}$ for the Appendix B frequency cutoff, written with the real part of its kernel; Hölder bounds are not included.
showcase.text: Let $g$ be an almost-everywhere strongly measurable, essentially bounded field on the unit-volume torus $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$, with values in a real normed space. Let $\Lambda>0$ and let $\psi$ be smooth and zero outside radius two. Define $H_\Lambda(z)=\sum_{|k|\le2\Lambda}\psi(k/\Lambda)e^{2\pi i k\cdot z}$ and $S^\mathbb R_\Lambda g(x)=\int_{\mathbb T^3}\operatorname{Re}H_\Lambda(x-z)g(z)\,dz$. The formal statement proves $\|S^\mathbb R_\Lambda g\|_{L^\infty}\le\|\check\psi\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^3)}\|g\|_{L^\infty}$. For an even symbol and a Banach target, this is the paper's multiplier. Without evenness, taking the real part symmetrizes the symbol. Completeness is not assumed in the formal estimate; its integral convention assigns zero for incomplete targets. The ordinary Banach-valued integral interpretation therefore uses a complete target. This construction uses the scalar spectral kernel, not a complexification of the target. No Hölder estimate is included.

showcase.why: Gives the weighted derivative, product and phase estimates (D.3)-(D.5) with explicit constants, and which normalized derivatives each one assumes bounded.
showcase.text: Fix a time set $I$, positive scales $\ell_*,h$ and $\gamma:I\to(0,\infty)$. For fields smooth in $(a,s)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, $\|f\|_{[n]}$ sums $\ell_*^{|\beta|}h^j\sup_{t,a,s}|\partial_a^\beta\partial_s^jf|$ over $|\beta|+j\le n$, once per multi-index. Assume the derivative families entering each right side below are bounded. The formal statement proves $\sum_i\|\partial_{a_i}f\|_{[n],\gamma}\le3\ell_*^{-1}\|f\|_{[n+1],\gamma}$, $\|\partial_sf\|_{[n],\gamma}\le h^{-1}\|f\|_{[n+1],\gamma}$, and $\|B(f,g)\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\|B\|\|f\|_{[n]}\|g\|_{[n],\gamma}$ for every continuous bilinear $B$. Weighted boundedness concerns derivatives of $f/\gamma$ or $g/\gamma$, not merely the unnormalized fields. For period-one Banach-valued fields, averaging, subtraction of the average and the zero-mean periodic primitive have respective bounds $1,2,2$ in the same norm; the primitive requires zero phase mean. All output derivative families are bounded. For phase-independent fields, the product estimate also holds with half-Hölder norms using the maximum of the uniform norm and seminorm. There is no time differentiation.

showcase.why: Lists what the auxiliary threshold condition requires of the stages and the terminal solution, kept separate from the theorem proving it.
showcase.text: The condition asks for one integer $b$, nondecreasing threshold $\mathcal B$ and lower bound $N_1$. For every $N\ge N_1$, it requires stages with $\lambda_0=N$, eventual velocity-residual time bounds, and eventual mixed correction bounds. Their activation times tend to a positive finite $T<S_j$ for every stage. It also requires a smooth odd maximal periodic Euler solution on $[0,T)$ with bounded velocity, $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$, and infinite time integrals of both $\|\nabla u\|_\infty$ and $\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_\infty$. Both $u$ and $\partial_tu$ have every local spatial derivative limit away from $\mathbb Z^3$. The velocity extends periodically and smoothly to all real times off that lattice, with no Euler requirement after $T$. These are required properties, not their existence proof. The displayed condition shares $T$ between stages and solution but does not require $U_j\to u$; the supplied assembly proof uses that actual limit.

summary: Alpöge, Buckmaster and Coiculescu build smooth odd periodic initial data whose Euler solution keeps bounded velocity while the vorticity at the origin becomes infinite at a finite time. A Craik–Criminale wave over a shear grows by a large factor and, at a suitable crossing time, supplies the shear that amplifies the next, higher-frequency wave. Each wave is localized near the origin with a profile that keeps its central gradient and bounds the pressure Hessian from above. Its error is removed in two parts: an endpoint problem chooses the initial value of the phase-mean correction, and a weighted transverse estimate controls the oscillation. A finite expansion, a time cutoff and a Fourier truncation leave a small residual, and one parameter schedule repeats the step indefinitely. The approximations converge to an exact Euler solution with the stated terminal behavior. Read the route to follow each step beside its formal statement.

route.statement:
There exist an odd divergence-free $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$, a finite time $0<T_*<\infty$, and a smooth odd velocity $u$ with smooth mean-zero pressure $p$ on $[0,T_*)	imes\mathbb T^3$, satisfying $u(0)=u_0$, $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u+
abla p=0$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$. The solution is maximal: no smooth Euler solution on a longer interval agrees with its velocity on $[0,T_*)$. Its velocity is uniformly bounded, while $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|	o\infty$ as $t\uparrow T_*$. Both $\int_0^{T_*}\|
abla u(t)\|_{L^\infty}\,dt$ and $\int_0^{T_*}\|\operatorname{curl}u(t)\|_{L^\infty}\,dt$ are infinite. For every compact $K\subset\mathbb T^3\setminus\{0\}$ and every integer $m\ge0$, both $u(t)$ and $\partial_tu(t)$ converge in $C^m(K)$.

The formal statement represents $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$ by integer-periodic fields on $\mathbb R^3$. It takes spatial essential suprema on $[-1/2,1/2]^3$, uses the Euclidean operator norm for $
abla u$, and expresses the divergent integrals as nonnegative Lebesgue integrals with value $\infty$. Avoiding the origin on the torus means avoiding every integer lattice point in this representation. Smoothness and Euler are required on the half-open time interval; the time derivative at zero is taken from the right. Local $C^m$ convergence means uniform convergence of the spatial derivatives through order $m$ to those of a $C^m$ field on a neighborhood of $K$.
route.explanation: The proof must keep the velocity bounded while its spatial derivatives become singular. It does this by adding localized oscillations with small velocity amplitude and large central gradient, then making their Euler residuals tend to zero. The formal theorem has the same content: it asserts a smooth odd divergence-free datum, a finite positive time and a smooth odd Euler solution with mean-zero pressure satisfying every displayed conclusion, and it adds that every maximal smooth solution from the same datum has the same lifespan and agrees with this one. Its representation of the torus, its norms and its local limits are those described above. Smooth extension in space and time through $T_*$ away from the origin is the additional assertion of Remark 1.2, established by a further choice of parameters.

route.statement: Let $D(t)$ be a smooth trace-free matrix on a time interval, with $D'+D^2$ symmetric. Let $F$ be smooth, odd and one-periodic, with $F'(0)=1$, and let $P$ be its one-periodic primitive with $\int_0^1P(s)\,ds=0$. Suppose the wave vector $k(t)\ne0$ and amplitude $\mathbf a(t)$ satisfy $k'=-D^Tk$, $\mathbf a'=-D\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}k$, $p_{\rm w}=2k\cdot D\mathbf a/|k|^2$, and $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$. Then $u(t,x)=D(t)x+\mathbf a(t)F(k(t)\cdot x)$ is a divergence-free Euler velocity on $\mathbb R^3$, with pressure $p(t,x)=-x\cdot(D'+D^2)x/2-p_{\rm w}P(k\cdot x)$. If $k$ and $\mathbf a$ are nonzero and perpendicular at one initial time, these properties persist at all later times for which the smooth background exists.
route.explanation: Perpendicularity makes the wave's quadratic self-advection vanish, while the two ordinary differential equations transport its phase and balance its remaining acceleration with pressure. Since $F'(0)=1$, the wave contributes the rank-one gradient $\mathbf a\otimes k$ at the origin; this is a consequence used later, not part of the lemma. The solution is exact over a spatially linear background on $\mathbb R^3$, and using its evolution along one trajectory of a spatially varying flow still requires the localization and correction argument, as Le Dizès and Leblanc explain for multifrequency solutions. The formal statement is stronger: it needs only a differentiable profile with a primitive, without oddness, periodicity, $F'(0)=1$ or a prescribed mean of $P$, and a background differentiable on a time interval. Its Euler identity also allows $k=0$, where the pressure coefficient is read as zero, and its persistence conclusion covers every time of the interval, including times before $t_0$.

route.statement: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, set $\varphi(\tau)=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ for normalized time $\tau\ge0$. The reference logarithmic growth rate solves $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)Y-Y^2$, $Y(0)=1$. It exists for all $\tau\ge0$, satisfies $|Y|\le1$, and has the representation $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$ with $0\le e(\tau)\le\varepsilon/8$. Its amplitude is $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp(\int_0^\tau Y(s)\,ds)=\sqrt{\cos\varphi(\tau)}\exp(\int_0^\tau(1+e(s))\cos\varphi(s)\,ds)$. There is exactly one zero $\tau_m$ of $Y$, with $2\le\varepsilon\tau_m\le3$; $Y$ is positive before it and negative afterwards. Consequently $a_{\rm ref}$ has its global maximum at $\tau_m$, and $\log a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)\ge\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1$.
route.explanation: The ratio $\varepsilon$ between the two positive couplings in the preceding wave's frame controls the available gain. A small ratio gives exponentially large growth before turning of the wave vector ends the reference growth. The selected physical wave will be compared with this reference solution; the displayed angle and maximizing time are not asserted to be those of the perturbed wave. The formal statement agrees with the lemma: it asserts existence and uniqueness of the solution on $[0,\infty)$, uses one function $e$ in both (2.13) and (2.14), and takes the derivative at $\tau=0$ from the right; nothing is asserted at negative times.

Choose $k_*\ne0$ and $0\le t_0<T$, put $\kappa=F^{-T}k_*$, and require $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda$. The nonzero central seed $\mathbf a\perp\kappa$ solves $\mathbf a_t=-M\mathbf a+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$, with $\max_{[t_0,T]}|\mathbf a(t,0)|=\lambda^{-3/4}$; put $\gamma(t)=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|$. Extend the seed to other labels with activation value $(I-P_{\kappa(t_0,a)})\mathbf a(t_0,0)$, where $P_\kappa=\kappa\otimes\kappa/|\kappa|^2$.

On the centered label cell, use the fixed smooth radial envelope $g(a)=\chi(|a|/\ell_*)$, where $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $[0,1]$ and $\chi=0$ on $[2,\infty)$, and the fixed smooth odd, one-periodic, zero-mean profile $F_h$ of Lemma 3.1. Set $A_1=g\mathbf aF_h$ and $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$, with a smooth cutoff $0\le\widetilde\chi\le1$ vanishing before $t_0$.

The norm $\|f\|_{[n]}$ sums $\ell_*^{|\alpha|}h^j\sup|\partial_a^\alpha\partial_s^j f|$ for $|\alpha|+j\le n$ over time, label and phase on the whole interval. The norm $\|f\|_{[n],\gamma}$ uses $[t_0,T]$ and divides the differentiated fields by $\gamma(t)>0$. These norms differentiate labels and phase, not time.
